Pregnancy

A chalazion during pregnancy: caring for an eyelid lump

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A chalazion is a lump caused by blockage and inflammation in an eyelid oil gland. It can happen during pregnancy, but not every swollen eyelid is a chalazion. Gentle care may help a confirmed uncomplicated lump, while pain, vision changes or signs of infection call for a different response.

What a chalazion feels like

The meibomian glands supply oil that helps the tear film protect the eye. When a gland becomes blocked, retained material can trigger a firm swelling in the upper or lower eyelid.

The area can be tender at first and later become a less painful lump. Watering or irritation may occur. A larger lump can press on the eye’s surface and affect vision.

A stye is another common eyelid problem, often with a more painful, localized infection. An optometrist or eye clinician can help distinguish them and check for other causes.

Pregnancy does not establish the cause

Hormonal changes can affect skin and eye comfort, but a lump should not automatically be blamed on pregnancy. There is not a clear basis for promising that every pregnancy-related chalazion will follow a particular course.

Underlying blepharitis, meibomian-gland dysfunction or rosacea may contribute to recurrence. Tell the clinician if your eyelids are often crusted, sore or irritated.

Having a chalazion is not proof of poor hygiene. Equally, saying that cleanliness never matters overlooks the role of gentle lid care in managing associated eyelid disease.

Seborrhoeic dermatitis can also accompany chronic eyelid inflammation. Diabetes or another condition affecting healing is useful information for the clinician, but a chalazion does not diagnose it. Unusual infectious causes are considered only when the history and examination suggest them; routine testing for tuberculosis or attributing every lump to viral conjunctivitis is not warranted.

Use comfortable warmth, not heat

Wash your hands and hold a clean, comfortably warm cloth against the closed eyelid. Rewarm it as needed without making it hot enough to burn.

Follow the duration and frequency suggested by your eye-care professional. Consistent gentle treatment is preferable to pressing harder or using very hot water.

After warming, gentle massage toward the eyelashes may help: downward on the upper lid and upward on the lower lid. Ask for a demonstration if you are unsure.

Do not squeeze the lump, puncture it, rub the eyeball or use an improvised instrument. Avoid eye makeup and contact lenses while the area is irritated or draining, and keep the area clean.

Warmth helps soften thickened gland secretions so they can drain more easily. The massage should move the lid gently toward its edge after warming, without squeezing the lump or pressing on the eye. This is aimed at the blocked gland, not at rubbing inflammation away.

Check medicines for your pregnancy

An uncomplicated chalazion is primarily an inflammatory blockage, so antibiotics are not automatically needed. A clinician may prescribe treatment for associated eyelid disease or spreading infection.

Tell the prescriber and pharmacist that you are pregnant before using an eye drop, ointment or oral medicine. Suitability depends on the actual product and reason for treatment.

Do not reuse someone else’s drops or an old prescription, and do not assume that an over-the-counter product can dissolve the lump. Steroid-containing eye treatments need professional supervision.

Pregnancy does not mean that all eye medicines are forbidden. The aim is to choose an appropriate treatment when there is a reason to use one.

Know when observation is no longer enough

Many chalazia improve over several weeks, but the time varies. Arrange review if the lump persists, recurs in the same place, grows or interferes with vision.

A persistent or atypical lesion may need specialist examination and sometimes a tissue sample. This does not mean that every recurrent chalazion is cancer.

Selected lumps can be treated with an injection or a small drainage procedure, often under local anaesthetic. The ophthalmologist should discuss the expected benefit, recurrence risk and pregnancy-specific treatment plan.

Never attempt drainage at home. If a procedure is planned, make sure the eye team and maternity team know about relevant medicines and pregnancy details.

Do not dismiss a new visual problem

Seek urgent assessment for marked or worsening eye pain, spreading hot swelling, fever, difficulty moving the eye or reduced vision. These can indicate a problem beyond an uncomplicated chalazion.

During pregnancy, new blurred vision or flashing lights also warrants prompt maternity advice, particularly with a severe headache or feeling unwell. Such symptoms can occur with pre-eclampsia and should not simply be attributed to an eyelid lump.

Sudden loss of vision or severe illness needs emergency care. When contacting the team, describe when symptoms started, whether one or both eyes are affected and whether the swelling is spreading.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Moorfields recommends warm compresses and gentle lid massage for a typical chalazion, with assessment of persistent or atypical lesions.

Antibiotics are not routine treatment for an uncomplicated blocked gland, and pregnancy suitability must be checked for any medicine or procedure.

How BeMama can help

Use comfortable warmth and clean hands, and arrange an eye review if the lump persists, returns in the same place or affects sight.

When to seek help

Eye pain, spreading hot swelling, fever or reduced vision needs urgent care; new visual disturbance in pregnancy also needs maternity advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Warm compresses and gentle lid care can help a confirmed uncomplicated chalazion.
  • Antibiotics and procedures are selected treatments, not automatic steps.
  • New visual symptoms in pregnancy need prompt assessment.

Frequently asked questions

Can I pop the lump to make it heal faster?

No. Squeezing or puncturing an eyelid lump can cause injury and infection.

Must I avoid all eye medicines while pregnant?

No. Have the exact product and reason for treatment checked by your clinician or pharmacist.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
